title: Notes from Above the Bookshop
subtitle: Lucía escribe en una revista de diseño sobre sus primeros meses como fundadora

paragraphs: When the editor of this magazine asked me to write about my first months as the founder of a design studio, my initial reaction was to say no. What I know about running a business could, until very recently, have been written on the back of a coffee receipt, and I suspect that anyone hoping for a confident guide to entrepreneurial success will be disappointed. What I can offer instead is something rather less polished: an honest account of what it has felt like to leave a secure job, sign a lease on an empty room above a bookshop, and discover, often the hard way, how much I didn't know.

It was in the summer of last year that the decision was effectively made, although at the time it felt more like the decision was making me. Helen Carter, who had founded Harbour Studio twenty years earlier at her kitchen table, announced that she was retiring. An American hotel group had offered to buy the studio, and she had turned them down. What she offered me instead was something I had never seriously considered: her blessing to set up on my own, together with the promise that she would not stand in the way of any clients who chose to follow me. I remember staring at the ceiling of our half-unpacked flat for most of that night. What kept me awake wasn't the work, which I knew I could do. It was the money, and the terrifying possibility that I had confused being good at my job with being good at running a company.

Had it not been for Daniel, I suspect I would have talked myself out of it. A developer by training and an optimist by temperament, he pointed out, with the slightly irritating calm of someone who has already made up his mind, that clients were already asking for me by name, and that I had never in my life done anything without a plan. Both observations were, annoyingly, correct. What he offered, though, was more than encouragement. It was a partnership. Within a month, he had handed in his notice at Harbour Studio, and the two of us were sitting in an estate agent's car, driving from one depressing office to another.

We must have seen seven offices before we found the one we now work in. It sits above an independent bookshop on Park Street, and the building, put up in 1890 and recently renovated, has the kind of tall windows that make you feel more creative than you actually are. Looking out of them on our first visit, I realised I could see the very street where I had got hopelessly lost on my first Saturday in Bristol, years earlier, with a map I couldn't read and an English I barely spoke. It seemed, if not exactly a sign, then at least a reasonably good omen. We signed the lease that afternoon, having read every single word of the contract twice, which in retrospect may have been the most sensible thing we did all year.

Choosing a name proved considerably harder than choosing an office. Having rejected, over several evenings, a long list of names that were either too clever, too dull or already taken, we eventually settled on Green Door Design. The name is a quiet tribute to Mrs Green, the landlady who opened her front door to me on my very first evening in this country, handed me a key and told me that everyone in the house was a friend. Of all the welcomes I have received in my life, that one remains the most important. She was, I'm told, so thrilled when she heard that she telephoned half of Clifton to tell them.

Nobody warns you how lonely the first weeks can be, even when you have a business partner. There is something unnerving about an office in which nothing happens unless you make it happen. At Harbour Studio, work arrived; at Green Door, we had to go out and find it. I spent much of January writing emails that nobody answered and redesigning our own website far more times than was strictly necessary. Rarely have I been so busy while achieving so little. Daniel, meanwhile, discovered an unexpected talent for assembling flat-pack furniture, which kept him cheerful, if not exactly productive.

What saved those weeks, in the end, was routine. Having spent years in an office where the day was shaped by other people's deadlines, I had to learn to shape my own. We began arriving at half past eight, as if someone might check. We introduced a Monday meeting, attended by exactly two people, at which we set ourselves three goals for the week and, on Friday, admitted honestly how many we had achieved. It sounds faintly absurd, and the bookshop owner downstairs, who could hear us through the floor, certainly found it entertaining. But it gave the days a structure, and structure, I discovered, is a surprisingly effective cure for panic.

Our first real client arrived in February, and it is no exaggeration to say that she changed everything. Grace Walker runs a chain of eco-friendly hostels, mainly for students and young travellers, and she came to our first meeting armed with a spreadsheet comparing our prices with those of every competitor in the south-west. It would appear, she observed politely, that we were rather more expensive than most. I remember feeling my face turn red. What I said in reply, after what felt like a very long pause, was that this might well be the case, but that good design tends to bring in considerably more bookings, and that we would be happy to prove it.

The proposal we eventually made was, with hindsight, the turning point. Rather than asking her to commit to a large project on the strength of a promise, we suggested a small pilot: a redesign of the booking system and website for a single hostel, at roughly a quarter of the full price. If the results were good, we would continue; if not, she would have lost relatively little. Daniel described our position as cautiously confident, which is probably the most accurate summary of our state of mind at the time. Privately, I was terrified. Had the pilot failed, I doubt the studio would have survived the spring.

It didn't fail. Within six weeks, online bookings at the pilot hostel had risen sharply, and Grace, who is not someone given to exaggeration, described the results as "frankly embarrassing for our previous agency". The full project followed. More remarkably, in April she offered to invest in the studio, provided that she was given a seat on the board and that we grew by thirty per cent over the following year. Not until I read the contract did I fully grasp what had happened: a stranger who had questioned our prices three months earlier now trusted us enough to put her own money into our future.

Those negotiations taught me more about business than anything I had read. I learned, for instance, that most conditions can be discussed, as long as you understand what the other person is actually worried about. Grace's main concern was not creative decisions, which she was happy to leave to us, but growth. Ours was independence. Once both concerns were on the table, a compromise was surprisingly easy to find. We kept creative control on condition that we met our targets; should we fail to do so, we agreed to sit down and talk rather than trigger any automatic penalty. It was, I think, a fair deal. But for her willingness to take a risk on two people with an empty office and a coffee machine, we would never have got this far.

Hiring our first employee raised a different set of questions. When you are a company of two, every new person changes the atmosphere entirely, and I found myself unexpectedly anxious about it. We needn't have advertised the position as widely as we did, as it turned out: Helen sent us three excellent CVs from people she had worked with, and we ended up choosing one of them. I would rather we had trusted her network from the start, rather than paying for an expensive advertisement that produced over two hundred applications, most of which had clearly been sent to every studio in the country. Lesson learned.

Not every lesson was so painless. Our most serious mistake, I would argue, was underestimating how long clients take to pay. A project finished in February may well not be paid for until April, and in the meantime rent, salaries and the electricity bill continue to arrive with impressive punctuality. There was one week in March when, having paid our new designer, we had enough money left in the account to cover roughly a fortnight. Nobody tells you that a company can be doing perfectly well on paper and still run out of cash. We have since introduced deposits, staged payments and a rather fierce reminder email, drafted by Daniel, which I suspect would frighten most of our clients if they ever received it.

I also underestimated, it must be said, how much I would miss the people at Harbour Studio. It is not only the conversations by the coffee machine, which never worked properly, but the feeling of belonging to something larger than yourself, with its jokes, its rituals and its shared complaints. Running your own studio means that, in a sense, you become the institution. There is nobody above you to blame when something goes wrong, and, more unsettlingly, nobody to tell you when you have done well. Helen, characteristically, anticipated this. On her last day she gave me a card that simply said: "Remember to tell yourself." It is pinned above my desk, next to a photograph of our first, very empty office, and on difficult days I find myself reading both more often than I would care to admit.

If I could give one piece of advice to anyone considering a similar step, it would be this: be honest about what you don't know, and find people who do. It was Helen who taught me how to price a project, Grace who taught me how to read a balance sheet, and Daniel who reminded me, usually at about eleven o'clock at night, that a business plan is a guide rather than a contract with the universe. I would also suggest, perhaps less obviously, that you keep the friends who knew you before. My former flatmates, a nurse and a musician, have no interest whatsoever in profit margins, which is precisely why their opinions about my life have proved so valuable.

There is a temptation, when writing a piece like this, to present the story as a neat progression from fear to success. The truth is messier. There have been weeks when I seriously wondered whether I had made a terrible mistake, and nights when I lay awake calculating how many months we could survive without new work. Some of those fears may well return. Next month we have been invited to present our work to a large hotel group in New York, the same company, as it happens, that once tried to buy Harbour Studio. Whether anything comes of it remains to be seen. Should they make an offer, I suspect the decision will be harder than anything I have described here.

What I can say with some confidence is that I no longer confuse fear with a lack of ability. The two feel remarkably similar at three in the morning, but they are not the same thing. Fear, I have come to believe, is mostly a sign that something matters. Little did I imagine, on that first evening at Mrs Green's door, with a suitcase and a phrasebook, that I would one day be writing these words in an office of my own, above a bookshop, with my name on the contract. It is not the ending I would have predicted. Then again, it isn't an ending at all.

questions.question: Why was Lucía initially reluctant to write the article?
options: She felt she knew too little about business to give confident advice.
She was too busy to write.
She didn't want to talk about Helen.

questions.question: What does Lucía mean by "it felt more like the decision was making me" (paragraph 2)?
options: She made the decision too quickly.
Circumstances seemed to push her towards it rather than her choosing freely.
Helen made the decision for her.

questions.question: What kept Lucía awake after Helen's offer?
options: Doubts about her design skills.
The noise in her new flat.
Fear that being good at design didn't mean she could run a company.

questions.question: Why does Lucía describe the view from the office window as "a reasonably good omen"?
options: It reminded her how far she had come since arriving in Bristol.
The street was full of design studios.
It was the street where Daniel lived.

questions.question: What is the tone of the sentence "Rarely have I been so busy while achieving so little" (paragraph 6)?
options: Bitter.
Self-mocking.
Proud.

questions.question: Why was the pilot project "the turning point"?
options: It was the most expensive project they had done.
It convinced Helen to invest.
It let Grace test the studio at low risk, and its success led to the full project.

questions.question: According to paragraph 10, what made the negotiation with Grace easier?
options: Understanding what each side was really worried about.
Letting Grace make the creative decisions.
Accepting automatic penalties.

questions.question: What does Lucía regret about hiring their first employee?
options: Choosing someone Helen recommended.
Spending money on a wide advertisement instead of using Helen's contacts.
Hiring too quickly.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the final paragraph?
options: She is certain the New York pitch will succeed.
Starting a business is mainly about luck.
Fear does not mean you lack ability; it shows that something matters.

exam_practice.title: Uso del inglés · Una palabra por hueco
exam_practice.instructions: Como en los exámenes oficiales: escribe una sola palabra en cada hueco.

items.text: It was in the summer ___ the decision was effectively made. ___ it not been for Daniel, I would have talked myself out of it. Rarely ___ I been so busy while achieving so little.
items.hint: Cleft: It was … that. Condicional sin if: Had it not been for…

items.text: ___ looked out of the window, I could see the street where I had got lost. ___ by the first person who welcomed me, we called the studio Green Door Design. Not ___ I read the contract did I grasp what had happened.
items.hint: Having + participio: acción anterior. Participio pasado con sentido pasivo: Inspired by…

items.text: We kept creative control on condition ___ we met our targets. ___ we fail to do so, we agreed to talk. ___ for her willingness to take a risk, we would never have got this far.
items.hint: Should + sujeto = if. But for + nombre = si no hubiera sido por.

exam_practice.title: Formación de palabras
exam_practice.instructions: Escribe una palabra derivada de la que está entre paréntesis (por ejemplo, DECIDE → decision).

items.text: The ___ (NEGOTIATE) with Grace taught me a great deal. Her ___ (WILLING) to take a risk changed everything. Our ___ (INDEPENDENT) mattered more to us than growth.
items.hint: Nombres con -tion, -ness, -ence: típicos del registro formal.

items.text: Daniel is an optimist by ___ (TEMPER). There is something ___ (NERVE) about an empty office. The results were, she said, ___ (FRANK) embarrassing for our previous agency.
items.hint: Un nombre con -ment; un prefijo negativo y -ing; un adverbio de actitud con -ly.

items.text: The building has been ___ (RECENT) renovated. Grace is not ___ (GIVE) to exaggeration. Online bookings rose ___ (SHARP) within six weeks.
items.hint: Be given to + nombre: tener tendencia a.

exam_practice.title: Transformaciones
exam_practice.instructions: Completa la segunda frase para que signifique lo mismo que la primera. Usa la palabra entre paréntesis sin cambiarla y entre dos y cinco palabras.

items.text: "We advertised widely, but it wasn't necessary." → We ___ (NEEDN'T) the position so widely.
items.explanation: Needn't have + participio: se hizo, pero no hacía falta.

items.text: "I wish we had trusted Helen's network from the start." → I ___ (RATHER) Helen's network from the start.
items.hint: Would rather + sujeto + past perfect para el pasado.

items.text: "I had no idea I would one day write these words." → Little ___ (DID) I would one day write these words.
"The money worried me, not the work." → It ___ (WAS) worried me, not the work.
"It is possible that some of those fears will return." → Some of those fears ___ (WELL) return.
items.hint: May well + verbo: es bastante probable.

items.text: "We had a pilot project, and that is why we survived." → If we hadn't had a pilot project, we ___ (WOULD) survived.

vocabulary.definition: a piece of paper that shows you have paid for something
a legal agreement to rent a building for a period of time
a sign of what will happen in the future
something that shows respect and admiration for someone
making you feel nervous or uncomfortable
a computer document with numbers in rows and columns
understanding a situation only after it has happened
a statement of what a company owns and owes
